newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica shares seen up next week, golds to sag.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica shares seen up next week, golds to sag.

text.p: South African shares, which passed a litmus test when exchange controls were relaxed this week, are seen firming next week as positive economic fundamentals buoy sentiment, analysts said on Friday.

They said nervousness over a flood of cash fleeing the country after individuals were allowed to invest offshore for the first time in 35 years on July 1, had abated and this should give way to increased confidence in the market next week.

"I think the market should do better next week. You haven't had this massive outflow of money. It's been quite small compared to what everyone expected," Denzil Newman, portfolio manager at Syfrets Managed Assets, told Reuters.

He said the rand, which touched a five-month low of 4.5425 against the dollar earlier this week, had stabilised and a bullish local bond market, which moved to its strongest levels in 17 months, would support the market next week.

"The rand is stabilising and that should bring some confidence back. If you look at the bond market it's still very strong, long rates are still coming down...but I wouldn't expect too much action," Newman added.

While strength was expected in the broader market, analysts said precious metal counters would still be shrouded in gloom in the wake of bullion's fall to a 12-year low on Thursday, which hacked more than three percent off the Johannesburg Stock Exchange's gold index on Friday.
Hit by news that the Reserve Bank of Australia sold 167 tonnes of gold in the first half of this year, bullion sagged to $323.70 in New York -- its lowest level since December 1985.
In London on Friday afternoon, it was fixed at $324.45 an ounce.
"It's only the metal prices that have been damaging us. I expect the mining side to be weaker again, but industrials are looking more comfortable to us," Newman said.
David Shapiro, director at stockbroking firm Societe Generale Frankel Pollak added:

"(The slump in the gold price) has got to have an impact on the economy and I think this is a sad thing. It still accounts for about 20 percent of our exports and therefore the price falling like this has an impact on our trade balance and our balance of payments."
"Because of it affecting our balance of payments, it's also going to perhaps delay any interest rate reduction," he told Reuters.
General consensus on interest rates amongst economists is for a one-point reduction in the second half of this year, with a total of three cuts expected by June next year.
"The equity market is now looking for that easing in monetary policy in order to have the desired effect on company earnings," one shares dealer added.

There will not be much for the market to chew on in the form of economic data next week -- the only key statistic out is the May producer price inflation (PPI) figure which will be released on Thursday at 0900 GMT.

A Reuters consensus poll of eight economists predicted overall PPI would rise 0.8 percent month-on-month or 8.4 percent year-on-year after April's 0.4 percent and 8.8 percent rise, as a stronger rand and a slowing economy continued to curb prices at the producer level.
There are no major South African corporate results due out next week.
